explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The writer says, “Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.” Peace and holiness come as a pair here, like dough and an oven. I'd say you've got a good grip on verse 14.

Success sounds nice, and I won't lie, I'd take a little. But the writer never mentions it in this verse. He says to pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness. Holiness is the one he says no one will see the Lord without.
Comfort is a tempting pick, friend. I spent years near a soft pile of paper and I know the appeal. But the writer doesn't list it. The verse says to pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness.

You got it, baker. The writer says a root of bitterness would “…cause trouble and defile many.” Notice the word many. One root, and it doesn't stay in one spot. I think that's why he tells them to watch out for each other.
Close to what a plant might do, but that's not what the writer says. He says the root springs up. Springing up is the opposite of withering. What it does is cause trouble and defile many.

explanations.answer: Stay small and hurt no one
explanations.explanation: I'd love that one, friend, a harmless little root. But the writer says the opposite. He says it springs up to cause trouble and defile many. That's why he opens with “See to it.”

Yes, a single meal. The writer says Esau “for a single meal sold his birthright.” Genesis 25:34 says Jacob, Esau's twin, gave him bread and lentil stew. That's one sitting, baker. A birthright is a LOT to trade for something that's gone by bedtime.

That number does show up in the Bible, but with someone else. Judas, one of Jesus' disciples, agreed to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:14-15). For Esau, the writer says “a single meal.” No silver involved.
A flock would at least be a real payment, friend. But the writer never mentions sheep here. He says Esau sold his birthright “for a single meal.” That's all he got.

True. The writer says Esau “could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears.” The tears are right there in verse 17. I think that makes this a heavy part to read, and I don't want to rush past it.

This one is true, baker. Verse 17 says Esau “could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears.” So the text says he did seek it, and with tears. It's an easy one to second-guess, because the verse starts so heavy.
That's it. The writer lists “darkness, gloom, and storm” right alongside the fire. Fire, dark and a storm all at once. Even I'd stay home with the oven mitts on.
Nice picture, friend, but the writer paints the opposite. He says the mountain is burning with fire, and that there's “darkness, gloom, and storm.” That's no calm sky.
That sounds like a lovely spot for a cookie break, baker. Not this mountain, though. The writer says it's burning with fire, with “darkness, gloom, and storm.” No picnic here.

Right, the word is stoned. The writer says the people could not bear what was commanded: “If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned.” It comes from Exodus 19:12-13. Even an animal. That tells you how serious the boundary was.

I get it, since the mountain is burning with fire. But the writer's word is stoned. He says, “If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned.” The fire is on the mountain, and the command is about stones.
Good guess, baker, because sacrifice is all over the Bible. But that isn't the word here. The writer says the animal “must be stoned.” That's what the people could not bear to hear.

Not quite, friend. Moses, Israel's leader, did not stay calm. The writer says the sight was so terrifying that even Moses said, “I am trembling with fear.” If Moses was shaking, I'd have been a puddle of dough.
False is right. The writer says the sight was so terrifying that even Moses, Israel's leader, said, “I am trembling with fear.” Even Moses. That word even says a lot, baker.

Yes, baker. The writer says, “Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.” After all that fire and storm, that word Instead feels like a deep breath. And I'll take a deep breath any day.
Carmel is a real mountain, friend, but this passage doesn't mention it. The writer says, “you have come to Mount Zion.” That's the one he names, and he pairs it with the city of the living God.
Hermon is a good mountain name, baker, and it sounds impressive. But it's not in this passage. The writer says, “you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.”

That's the word. The writer says you have come to “the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven.” Enrolled, like a name written down on a list. I think there's something comforting about being on that list, friend.
Egypt is a big name in the Bible, friend, but it isn't here. The writer says the congregation of the firstborn is “enrolled in heaven.” That's where the enrolling happens.
Bethlehem is a fine town to know, baker, but the verse points higher. It says the congregation of the firstborn is “enrolled in heaven.” That's the blank to fill.

explanations.answer: The mediator of a new covenant
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The writer says you have come “to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant.” A mediator stands between two sides. A new covenant also means something new is happening. That's good news after that scary mountain.

explanations.answer: The builder of a new temple
explanations.explanation: That's a creative one, friend, but the writer doesn't say it. He calls Jesus “the mediator of a new covenant.” No temple blueprints in this verse.

explanations.answer: The keeper of the old law
explanations.explanation: I see where that comes from, baker, since the old mountain is in the verses before. But the writer calls Jesus “the mediator of a new covenant.” The word is new, not old.

True, baker. The writer says you have come to “the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.” Abel was Adam's son, and God told Cain, Abel's brother, “Your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10). So both bloods speak, and the writer says one speaks better.

That's true, friend. The writer says the sprinkled blood “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.” Abel was Adam's son, and his blood cried out from the ground (Genesis 4:10). The writer sets the two side by side and says the sprinkled blood speaks the better word.

Yes, baker. The writer says, “how much less will we escape if we reject Him who warns us from heaven?” So the people did not escape when they refused Him on earth, and the writer says it's even less for us if we reject Him from heaven. It's a serious line, so I'm not going to joke on it.

That's the opposite of what the writer says, friend. He says, “how much less will we escape if we reject Him who warns us from heaven?” The people did not escape when they refused Him on earth. So it isn't easier for us.

explanations.answer: We will get a second warning
explanations.explanation: A second warning would be nice, baker, like a snooze button. But the writer doesn't say that. He says, “how much less will we escape if we reject Him who warns us from heaven?”

Not this time, friend. The writer quotes the promise as “Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well.” That little phrase, “but heaven as well,” is the part that's easy to miss. So it's more than the earth.
False is right, baker. The promise says, “Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well.” So the earth is shaken, and heaven as well. The word only would break the verse.

That's the word. The writer says “Once more” signifies the removal of what can be shaken, “so that the unshakable may remain.” The shaken things are created things. What's left is the unshakable. I'd say that's a good thing to be holding onto.
Faithful is a good word, friend, but it isn't the one in this verse. The writer says the removal happens “so that the unshakable may remain.” The blank wants the word that goes with shaking.
Chosen has a nice ring, baker, but it isn't what the writer says here. The verse says created things are removed “so that the unshakable may remain.” The shaking is what sets up the word.

That's it, baker. The writer says, “let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe.” Notice the order. Gratitude comes first, and the worship follows from it. I like that.
That sounds peaceful, friend, but the writer doesn't say it. He says to worship God “acceptably with reverence and awe.” Silence and fasting aren't in this verse.

I'd sign up for that one, baker, and I'd be the loudest one in the room. But it's not what the writer says. He says to worship God “acceptably with reverence and awe.” Music and dancing aren't named here.
